concepts.title: Event loop, libuv and the thread pool
concepts.summary: Your JavaScript runs on one thread. libuv polls the OS for network I/O, and a pool of four threads ({{UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE}}) handles file system, DNS lookup, crypto and zlib. Anything synchronous on the main thread delays every other request.
concepts.production: A 40 MB {{JSON.parse}} on a reporting endpoint froze a pod for 300 ms, and every other user's request queued behind it.
concepts.interview: Name the phases, then say where microtasks and {{process.nextTick}} run. That separates people who memorised from people who have debugged.

concepts.title: ESM, CommonJS and interop
concepts.summary: ESM uses import and export, is statically analysable and allows top-level await. CommonJS uses {{require()}} and is synchronous. Set {{"type": "module"}}, import built-ins with the {{node:}} prefix, use {{import.meta.dirname}}, and know that recent LTS lines can {{require()}} ESM that has no top-level await.
concepts.production: A library loaded once as ESM and once as CJS creates two copies of its module state (the dual package hazard), so a singleton cache silently splits.
concepts.interview: Explain why {{__dirname}} is missing in ESM and what the {{exports}} map in package.json controls.

concepts.title: Release lines and the LTS policy
concepts.summary: Run Active or Maintenance LTS in production. Node 20 reached end of life on 30 April 2026. Node 24 is Active LTS (end of life April 2028), Node 22 is in Maintenance (April 2027) and Node 26 becomes LTS on 28 October 2026. From Node 27 there is one major a year and every release becomes LTS.
concepts.production: Teams on an end-of-life runtime stop getting security patches and eventually lose support from base images and serverless platforms.
concepts.interview: State an upgrade policy: test the Current line in CI, move production to LTS within a few months, fail CI on new deprecation warnings.

concepts.title: Built-ins that replace packages
concepts.summary: Modern Node ships {{fetch}}, {{AbortSignal.timeout}}, {{structuredClone}}, {{node:test}}, {{--watch}}, {{--env-file}}, {{util.parseArgs}} and {{crypto.randomUUID}}. Each removes a dependency, and every dependency removed shrinks your attack surface.
concepts.production: One service dropped node-fetch, dotenv, nodemon and uuid and lost four direct dependencies plus dozens of transitive ones.
concepts.interview: Show that you reach for the platform first and add a package only when it earns its place.

concepts.title: package.json: exports, engines and lockfiles
concepts.summary: {{exports}} defines public entry points and blocks deep imports. {{engines}} documents supported Node versions. The lockfile pins the whole tree, and CI should install with {{npm ci}} so builds are reproducible.
concepts.production: A deep import of another team's internal file broke on a minor release because nothing declared it public.
concepts.interview: Explain ^ versus ~ versus exact versions, and why {{npm install}} and {{npm ci}} behave differently.

concepts.title: Running TypeScript natively (type stripping)
concepts.summary: Node can run {{.ts}} files by erasing types without transpiling. It is stable in Node 26 and runs without a flag in newer 22.x and 24.x releases. Only erasable syntax works: no enums, namespaces or parameter properties, and no path aliases. Use {{import type}} and the {{erasableSyntaxOnly}} option, and still run {{tsc --noEmit}} to type-check.
concepts.production: Scripts, migrations and small services run directly with no build step; larger services still build for source maps, bundling and startup time.
concepts.interview: Know the trade-off: faster iteration against losing build-time transforms, and that stripping does not type-check.

concepts.title: Permission Model and Single Executable Apps
concepts.summary: The opt-in Permission Model ({{--permission}} with {{--allow-fs-read}} and similar flags) restricts file system, child process and worker access. Single Executable Apps bundle a script into the node binary for CLIs and agents.
concepts.production: A CLI shipped to customers as one binary with no runtime install; a build script ran under the permission flag so a hijacked dependency could not read the home directory.
concepts.interview: Call it defence in depth, not a sandbox. Interviewers listen for whether you overstate it.

concepts.title: Closures, scope and this
concepts.summary: A closure keeps the variables of the scope where it was created. {{this}} depends on how a function is called, not where it is written. Arrow functions capture {{this}} lexically.
concepts.production: A retry helper built in a loop with {{var}} logged the same attempt number every time until it was changed to {{let}}.
concepts.interview: Predict the output of closures in loops and of a detached method such as {{const f = obj.method}}.

concepts.title: Iterators, generators and async iterators
concepts.summary: {{for await}} consumes streams and paged APIs lazily, one item at a time. An async generator turns cursor pagination into a simple loop, and iterator helpers such as {{map}} and {{take}} are available in modern Node.
concepts.production: An export job walked 2 million rows through an async generator instead of loading them all into memory.
concepts.interview: Write an async generator that follows a {{nextCursor}} until it is empty.

concepts.title: TypeScript strictness for backends
concepts.summary: Turn on {{strict}}, {{noUncheckedIndexedAccess}} and {{verbatimModuleSyntax}}, and use {{module: nodenext}} so TypeScript matches Node's real resolution rules. Types vanish at runtime, so strictness catches mistakes only in code you control.
concepts.production: {{noUncheckedIndexedAccess}} exposed three places that assumed {{arr[0]}} always exists, each a production crash waiting for an empty result.
concepts.interview: Explain what {{strict}} adds and why TypeScript alone cannot protect you from bad JSON.

concepts.title: Validate at the boundary: Zod and inferred types
concepts.summary: Parse untrusted input once at the edge with a schema library such as Zod or Valibot, then derive the static type from the schema so the two never drift. Inside the boundary you can trust the types.
concepts.production: A mobile client sent a string for a number. Without validation it reached the database layer and surfaced as a confusing SQL error.
concepts.interview: Say where validation lives (HTTP, queue consumers, env vars) and why it is not only for HTTP bodies.

concepts.title: Discriminated unions and exhaustive checks
concepts.summary: Model states as a union tagged by one field, then switch on it. Assigning the leftover value to {{never}} makes the compiler fail when someone adds a new state and forgets to handle it.
concepts.production: Modelling a payment as pending, captured or refunded made the impossible state "refunded but never captured" unrepresentable.
concepts.interview: Show how a union replaces a bag of optional fields and booleans.

concepts.title: Dates, time zones and Temporal
concepts.summary: {{Date}} is mutable and mixes UTC with local time. Store instants in UTC, convert at the edge, and prefer Temporal, which is enabled by default in Node 26. Never build dates from ambiguous strings.
concepts.production: A billing cron fired an hour early twice a year because it computed "midnight" in local time across a daylight saving change.
concepts.interview: Be able to explain why {{new Date('2026-03-01')}} is UTC but {{new Date('2026-03-01T00:00')}} is local.

concepts.title: Microtasks, nextTick and the order of output
concepts.summary: After each macrotask Node drains {{process.nextTick}} callbacks first, then promise microtasks, before moving on. {{setImmediate}} runs in the check phase. Starving the microtask queue blocks I/O completely.
concepts.production: A recursive promise chain that never yielded stalled all HTTP responses on a worker until it was broken up with {{setImmediate}}.
concepts.interview: Be ready to order a mixed snippet of {{setTimeout}}, {{setImmediate}}, promises and nextTick.

concepts.title: Promise combinators and unhandled rejections
concepts.summary: {{Promise.all}} fails fast, {{allSettled}} reports every result, {{race}} takes the first to settle and {{any}} the first to succeed. Since Node 15 an unhandled rejection crashes the process by default.
concepts.production: A fire-and-forget audit call rejected and took down a pod, because nothing awaited or caught it.
concepts.interview: Explain why a missing {{await}} inside {{try/catch}} lets the error escape.

concepts.title: Concurrency limits and backpressure
concepts.summary: {{Promise.all}} over 10,000 items opens 10,000 sockets. Cap work with a pool (p-limit style) or process in batches, and let streams and queues apply backpressure instead of buffering everything.
concepts.production: A migration script fired 20,000 parallel requests, exhausted the downstream rate limit and was banned for an hour.
concepts.interview: Implement a concurrency limiter on a whiteboard. It is in the code lab below.

concepts.title: AbortController, timeouts and cancellation
concepts.summary: {{AbortSignal.timeout(ms)}} and {{AbortSignal.any([...])}} give one cancellation signal that you pass through {{fetch}}, {{timers/promises}}, streams and drivers that support it. When a client disconnects, stop the work behind it.
concepts.production: A slow downstream made requests pile up for 60 seconds each. A 2 second timeout with a signal freed the workers.
concepts.interview: Say that every network call needs a timeout and that cancellation should propagate, not just the first hop.
concepts.code: const res = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) });

concepts.title: AsyncLocalStorage for request context
concepts.summary: {{AsyncLocalStorage}} carries data such as a request id, tenant or transaction across awaits without passing it through every function. It powers log correlation and tracing libraries.
concepts.production: Every log line from one request shared a request id, so support could trace a failed checkout in seconds.
concepts.interview: Know the risk: context leaks if you run work outside the store, for example in a callback registered at startup.

concepts.title: Streams, pipeline and backpressure
concepts.summary: Streams process data in chunks. {{stream/promises}} {{pipeline}} wires them together, propagates errors and destroys every stream on failure. Backpressure pauses a fast producer when a slow consumer cannot keep up.
concepts.production: Piping a 4 GB export straight from the database to the HTTP response kept memory flat instead of buffering it.
concepts.interview: Explain what {{highWaterMark}} is and why {{.pipe()}} alone leaks on error.

concepts.title: Worker threads, child processes and cluster
concepts.summary: Use worker threads for CPU work inside one process, child processes to run other programs or isolate crashes, and cluster or more containers to use more cores for I/O. Piscina-style pools avoid creating a worker per task.
concepts.production: Image resizing moved to a worker pool, so the API thread stayed responsive during bursts.
concepts.interview: Give one sentence on when to prefer more containers over cluster in Kubernetes.

concepts.title: Event loop lag and timers
concepts.summary: {{setTimeout}} is a minimum delay, not a promise. Measure event loop delay with {{perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay}} and alert on it, because it reveals blocking work before users complain. Call {{unref()}} on housekeeping timers so they do not keep the process alive.
concepts.production: An alert on event loop p99 above 100 ms caught a regex regression minutes after deploy.
concepts.interview: Name the metric you would graph to detect a blocked loop.

concepts.title: HTTP semantics, status codes and pagination
concepts.summary: Methods have meaning: GET is safe, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST is neither by default. Use status codes precisely (401 versus 403, 409 for conflicts, 422 for semantic validation) and prefer cursor pagination for large or changing data.
concepts.production: Offset pagination skipped and duplicated rows while new orders arrived; a cursor on {{(created_at, id)}} fixed it.
concepts.interview: Explain PUT versus PATCH, and why offset pagination degrades.

concepts.title: Caching: Cache-Control, ETag and CDNs
concepts.summary: {{Cache-Control}} sets freshness, {{ETag}} with {{If-None-Match}} lets clients revalidate cheaply, and {{Vary}} tells caches which request headers change the response. A CDN in front removes load for public data.
concepts.production: Adding ETags to a product catalogue turned most requests into small 304 responses and cut egress cost.
concepts.interview: Say which responses must never be cached ({{Cache-Control: private}} or {{no-store}}).

concepts.title: Idempotency keys and safe retries
concepts.summary: Clients retry on timeouts. A client-supplied {{Idempotency-Key}} lets the server store the first result and replay it, so a second attempt cannot charge a card twice. Enforce with a unique constraint, not just a check.
concepts.production: A flaky mobile network caused duplicate orders until the checkout endpoint required an idempotency key.
concepts.interview: Describe the three states: new, in progress, completed. The code lab has a middleware.

concepts.title: Errors as a contract: problem details
concepts.summary: RFC 9457 defines {{application/problem+json}} with {{type}}, {{title}}, {{status}}, {{detail}} and {{instance}}. A consistent error shape lets clients handle failures generically and keeps stack traces out of responses.
concepts.production: Support tickets dropped once every service returned the same error shape with a stable {{type}} URL clients could branch on.
concepts.interview: Know which errors are the client's fault (4xx) and which should alert you (5xx).

concepts.title: OpenAPI and contract-first design
concepts.summary: Treat the OpenAPI document as the source of truth. Generate types, validators, docs and client SDKs from it, and diff it in CI to catch breaking changes before release.
concepts.production: A generated client replaced three hand-written ones and removed a class of mismatched field names.
concepts.interview: Contrast contract-first with code-first and name one tool that checks for breaking changes.

concepts.title: API versioning and deprecation
concepts.summary: Put the major version in the URL for public APIs, keep changes inside a major additive, and retire old versions with {{Deprecation}} and {{Sunset}} headers plus a published window. Use expand and contract for renames.
concepts.production: A partner stayed on v1 for two years until brownouts and direct outreach moved them.
concepts.interview: Define breaking versus non-breaking changes in two sentences and give three examples of each.

concepts.title: Webhooks: signatures, retries and ordering
concepts.summary: Verify an HMAC signature over the raw body with a timing-safe compare, reject old timestamps, acknowledge quickly with 2xx and process asynchronously. Providers retry and can deliver out of order, so handlers must be idempotent.
concepts.production: Parsing JSON before verifying the signature changed the bytes, so valid webhooks failed until the raw body was captured.
concepts.interview: Explain how you handle duplicate and out-of-order events.

concepts.title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC or tRPC
concepts.summary: REST fits public, cacheable resources. GraphQL fits varied client needs but needs DataLoader and query cost limits. gRPC fits low-latency internal calls with protobuf contracts. tRPC fits TypeScript monorepos where one team owns client and server.
concepts.production: A mobile team needed three screens from one round trip, which justified GraphQL for that surface only.
concepts.interview: Pick by constraints (consumers, caching, language mix), not fashion.

concepts.title: Keep-alive, connection reuse and 502s
concepts.summary: Reuse connections with keep-alive agents or undici pools. Node's default {{server.keepAliveTimeout}} is 5 seconds, which can be shorter than a load balancer's idle timeout, producing sporadic 502s when the balancer reuses a socket Node just closed.
concepts.production: Sporadic 502s with no application errors disappeared after raising {{keepAliveTimeout}} above the balancer idle timeout.
concepts.interview: Give this as your example of a bug visible only at the network layer.

concepts.title: Express, Fastify, NestJS and Hono
concepts.summary: Express is minimal and ubiquitous (Express 5 forwards rejected promises). Fastify is schema-first with built-in validation, logging and plugins. NestJS adds modules and dependency injection on top of Express or Fastify. Hono is small, built on web-standard Request and Response, and runs on Node, edge runtimes and Bun.
concepts.production: A team of twelve chose NestJS for its conventions; a latency-sensitive gateway chose Fastify; an edge function used Hono.
concepts.interview: Choose on team size, conventions and runtime target, not on hello-world benchmarks.

concepts.title: Layered, hexagonal and clean architecture
concepts.summary: Keep the domain independent of frameworks. Define ports (interfaces the domain needs) and adapters (HTTP, database, queue) that implement them. Dependencies point inward, so you can test the domain without a server or database.
concepts.production: Swapping an email provider touched one adapter file and no business logic.
concepts.interview: Draw the dependency direction and say what you gain and what extra code it costs.

concepts.title: Dependency injection and the composition root
concepts.summary: Pass collaborators in through constructors or function arguments, and wire everything in one place at startup. A container such as NestJS DI or awilix is optional; plain factories work for most services.
concepts.production: Tests replaced the payment client with a fake by passing it into one factory.
concepts.interview: Explain DI without naming a framework.

concepts.title: Modular monolith before microservices
concepts.summary: One deployable with enforced module boundaries (no cross-module imports, explicit public APIs) gets most of the benefit of services without distributed-system costs. Split a module out only when scaling, ownership or release cadence demands it.
concepts.production: A six-person team ran fourteen services and spent more time on deploy plumbing than features; consolidating into modules cut toil.
concepts.interview: Say what signals justify splitting, and what you pay for it (network failures, consistency, observability).

concepts.title: Config and the twelve-factor app
concepts.summary: Read configuration from environment variables, validate it at startup, and fail fast if it is wrong. Keep one build artifact for every environment, treat logs as streams and keep processes stateless.
concepts.production: A missing variable was discovered only when a rarely used code path ran in production; startup validation would have caught it at deploy.
concepts.interview: Describe how you validate config and keep secrets out of the repository.

concepts.title: Monorepos and workspaces
concepts.summary: Workspaces in pnpm or npm share dependencies and local packages. Turborepo or Nx add task graphs and remote caching so only affected packages rebuild, and Changesets manage versioning and changelogs.
concepts.production: Sharing a validation package between API and web removed a class of drift bugs and cut CI time through caching.
concepts.interview: Know when a monorepo hurts: unclear ownership and slow CI without caching.

concepts.title: Domain-driven design essentials
concepts.summary: Bounded contexts keep models consistent inside a boundary, aggregates enforce invariants in one transaction, and domain events announce what happened. An anti-corruption layer protects your model from messy external APIs.
concepts.production: Separating Billing and Fulfilment contexts stopped one team's new field from rippling through the other's code.
concepts.interview: Use it to justify service boundaries, not as vocabulary.

concepts.title: PostgreSQL transactions, isolation and locks
concepts.summary: Postgres defaults to READ COMMITTED. Use {{SELECT ... FOR UPDATE}} to lock rows you will change, {{SKIP LOCKED}} to build safe job queues, and consistent lock ordering to avoid deadlocks. Higher isolation prevents anomalies at the cost of retries.
concepts.production: Two workers charged the same invoice until the row was locked with {{FOR UPDATE}} inside the transaction.
concepts.interview: Explain a lost update and two ways to prevent it.

concepts.title: Indexes and reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE
concepts.summary: A B-tree index speeds lookups and sorts. Column order matters in composite indexes, partial and covering indexes save space and reads, and every index slows writes. {{EXPLAIN ANALYZE}} shows what actually happened.
concepts.production: A query went from 2 seconds to 8 ms after a composite index matched its filter and sort.
concepts.interview: Read a plan aloud: scan type, row estimates versus actual, and where time goes.

concepts.title: Connection pooling and the budget
concepts.summary: Each pod has its own pool, so pods times pool size must stay under the database's {{max_connections}}. A pooler such as PgBouncer multiplexes many clients over few connections. Serverless functions need it most.
concepts.production: Autoscaling to 40 pods with pools of 20 produced "too many clients" until a connection budget and PgBouncer were added.
concepts.interview: Do the multiplication in the interview.

concepts.title: ORMs and query builders: Prisma, Drizzle, Kysely
concepts.summary: ORMs speed up CRUD and migrations but can hide N+1 queries. Query builders such as Kysely and Drizzle keep SQL visible with typed results. Whichever you choose, you must be able to read the SQL it generates and drop to raw SQL when needed.
concepts.production: A list endpoint issued 101 queries through an ORM include until the relation was fetched with a join.
concepts.interview: Defend your choice with trade-offs: type safety, escape hatches, migration story.

concepts.title: Zero-downtime migrations
concepts.summary: Use expand and contract: add a nullable column, deploy code that writes both, backfill in small batches, switch reads, then drop the old column. Create indexes concurrently and avoid long exclusive locks on busy tables.
concepts.production: A plain {{ALTER TABLE}} locked a hot table for minutes; the same change split into safe steps caused no interruption.
concepts.interview: Walk through renaming a column with no downtime.

concepts.title: Caching with Redis: patterns and stampedes
concepts.summary: Cache-aside is the default: read the cache, fall back to the database, then fill. Add TTL jitter, single-flight or locks so one miss does not trigger a thousand queries, and decide how invalidation works before you cache.
concepts.production: Keys expiring together at 03:00 sent the database to 100 percent CPU until TTLs were jittered and refreshes coalesced.
concepts.interview: Say what you do when Redis is down: the service should degrade, not fail.

concepts.title: MongoDB modelling
concepts.summary: Embed data that is read together and bounded in size; reference data that is shared or unbounded. Index for your queries, validate with schemas, and remember transactions exist but fit documents less naturally than rows.
concepts.production: An unbounded array of comments inside a post document hit the 16 MB limit and slowed every read.
concepts.interview: Give the embed versus reference rule and one case that breaks it.

concepts.title: Consistency, CAP and replica lag
concepts.summary: Under a partition you trade consistency for availability. Read replicas lag, so a user may not see their own write. Route read-your-writes traffic to the primary or use session stickiness, and design for eventual consistency where it is acceptable.
concepts.production: Profile updates appeared to revert for a second until reads right after a write were pinned to the primary.
concepts.interview: Explain read-your-writes in one sentence and a fix.

concepts.title: Choosing the right store
concepts.summary: Postgres covers most needs, including JSON and vectors via extensions. Add Redis for caching and counters, a search engine for relevance queries, a column store for analytics and DynamoDB when access patterns are known and scale is extreme. Feed secondary stores through an outbox or change stream.
concepts.production: Search ran on Postgres full-text until relevance tuning demanded OpenSearch, fed by change events.
concepts.interview: Resist adding stores without a measured need.

concepts.title: Queues versus logs: SQS, RabbitMQ and Kafka
concepts.summary: Queues deliver each message to one worker and delete it when acknowledged. Logs like Kafka keep an ordered record that many consumer groups can replay. Choose a queue for work distribution and a log for event streams and replay.
concepts.production: Order events fed analytics, search and email from one Kafka topic, each with its own consumer group.
concepts.interview: Contrast the two and state where ordering is guaranteed (per partition).

concepts.title: At-least-once delivery and idempotent consumers
concepts.summary: Brokers redeliver on timeout or crash, so handlers see duplicates. Make handlers idempotent by recording processed message ids or using unique constraints and upserts. Exactly-once effects come from at-least-once plus idempotency.
concepts.production: A redelivered "send email" message sent two receipts until the handler stored the message id first.
concepts.interview: Say why "exactly once" in marketing copy has an asterisk.

concepts.title: Retries, backoff, jitter and dead-letter queues
concepts.summary: Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter, cap attempts, and move poison messages to a dead-letter queue with an alert. Never retry forever and never block the queue on one bad message.
concepts.production: One malformed message blocked a consumer for hours until a retry limit and DLQ were added.
concepts.interview: Describe retry policy per error class: transient, permanent, unknown.

concepts.title: Outbox and inbox patterns
concepts.summary: Write the business change and an outbox row in one database transaction, then a relay publishes outbox rows to the broker. This removes the dual-write problem where the database commits but the publish fails. The inbox pattern dedupes on the consumer side.
concepts.production: Orders were saved but "order created" events were sometimes lost after a broker blip, until an outbox relay replaced direct publishing.
concepts.interview: Draw the transaction boundary and explain why publishing inside the handler is unsafe.

concepts.title: Sagas: orchestration versus choreography
concepts.summary: A saga is a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions instead of one distributed transaction. Orchestration uses a coordinator that tells each step what to do; choreography lets services react to each other's events.
concepts.production: A checkout saga reserved stock, charged the card and booked shipping, refunding and releasing stock if a later step failed.
concepts.interview: Say when orchestration is easier to reason about and monitor.

concepts.title: Ordering, partitions and consumer groups
concepts.summary: Kafka orders messages only within a partition. Choose a key (such as order id) so related events share a partition. A consumer group splits partitions among members, and a rebalance briefly pauses consumption.
concepts.production: Updates for one customer arrived out of order until the customer id became the partition key.
concepts.interview: Explain how many consumers you can usefully run for N partitions.

concepts.title: Background jobs and scheduling with BullMQ
concepts.summary: BullMQ on Redis offers delayed, repeatable and rate-limited jobs with retries and concurrency control. Make every job idempotent, set timeouts, monitor stalled jobs and run schedulers in one place so cron work does not execute on every pod.
concepts.production: A nightly report ran N times, once per pod, until scheduling moved to a single repeatable job.
concepts.interview: Say how you avoid double execution and how you observe queue depth.

concepts.title: OWASP API Security Top 10
concepts.summary: The most common API failure is broken object level authorization: authenticated users reading other people's objects by changing an id. Also watch mass assignment, excessive data exposure, missing rate limits and unsafe consumption of third-party APIs.
concepts.production: Changing {{/orders/1001}} to {{/orders/1002}} returned another customer's order because the handler checked login but not ownership.
concepts.interview: Lead with object level authorization. It is the answer most interviewers want.

concepts.title: Authentication: sessions, JWT and OIDC
concepts.summary: Use short-lived access tokens and rotating refresh tokens, or server-side sessions with secure cookies. JWT pitfalls: accepting the {{none}} algorithm, no revocation, storing in {{localStorage}}, and putting secrets in the payload. Use OAuth 2.0 with PKCE and OpenID Connect for login with an identity provider.
concepts.production: A leaked long-lived JWT could not be revoked until access tokens were shortened and refresh tokens became rotating.
concepts.interview: Explain refresh token rotation and what you do on suspected token theft.

concepts.title: Passkeys and WebAuthn
concepts.summary: Passkeys use public-key cryptography bound to the site's origin, so they resist phishing and password reuse. The server stores a public key and verifies signatures; libraries such as SimpleWebAuthn handle the ceremony.
concepts.production: Offering passkeys cut password reset tickets and removed credential stuffing as an attack route for opted-in users.
concepts.interview: Say why phishing-resistant authentication matters more after the 2025 npm maintainer phishing attacks.

concepts.title: Authorization models: RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC
concepts.summary: RBAC grants permissions through roles, ABAC evaluates attributes such as department and resource owner, and ReBAC follows relationships such as "member of the team that owns this folder". Centralise decisions in one layer and consider Postgres row-level security as a backstop.
concepts.production: Scattered {{if (user.role === 'admin')}} checks diverged until policy moved into one authorization module.
concepts.interview: Pick a model for a given product and justify it.

concepts.title: Input handling: injection, path traversal and SSRF
concepts.summary: Use parameterised queries, never string-built SQL. Beware NoSQL operator injection like {{ {"$ne": null} }}, shell injection with {{exec}} (prefer {{execFile}} with an argument array), path traversal through user-supplied file names and server-side request forgery through user-supplied URLs.
concepts.production: An image-fetch feature let users request internal metadata addresses until URLs were checked against an allow-list and private ranges were blocked.
concepts.interview: Give one defence for each of SQL injection, path traversal and SSRF.

concepts.title: Prototype pollution and ReDoS
concepts.summary: Merging untrusted objects can write {{__proto__}} or {{constructor}} and poison every object. Block those keys, use {{Object.create(null)}} or validated schemas. A backtracking regular expression on hostile input can pin the single thread, which is how a 2019 Cloudflare outage happened.
concepts.production: A pathological email regex took 10 seconds on a crafted string and stalled the whole worker.
concepts.interview: Explain why regexes are a denial-of-service risk specifically in a single-threaded runtime.

concepts.title: Supply-chain security
concepts.summary: Commit the lockfile and install with {{npm ci}}. Review new dependencies, disable install scripts where you can ({{--ignore-scripts}}), verify provenance with {{npm audit signatures}}, delay adopting brand-new releases (Renovate {{minimumReleaseAge}}), use phishing-resistant 2FA for publishing and give CI tokens the least privilege.
concepts.production: In September 2025 maintainer phishing pushed malicious versions of widely used packages for hours, and a self-replicating worm followed. Teams with pinned lockfiles and release-age delays avoided most exposure.
concepts.interview: Describe your dependency policy in five bullet points.

concepts.title: Secrets management
concepts.summary: Keep secrets out of the repository, images and logs. Load them from a cloud secret manager at runtime, prefer short-lived credentials (for example OIDC federation from CI to cloud) and rotate on a schedule and after any suspected exposure.
concepts.production: A leaked access key in a public repository was abused within minutes; moving to role-based access removed long-lived keys altogether.
concepts.interview: Say what you do in the first hour after discovering a leaked secret.

concepts.title: Rate limiting and abuse protection
concepts.summary: Limit per user, per API key and per IP using a token bucket or sliding window stored in Redis so limits hold across pods. Throttle login attempts, return {{429}} with {{Retry-After}} and add WAF or bot rules at the edge.
concepts.production: Credential stuffing was stopped by per-account and per-IP limits plus an alert on failed-login ratio.
concepts.interview: Explain why in-memory limiters fail behind more than one instance.

concepts.title: Headers, CORS and CSRF
concepts.summary: Use {{helmet}} for secure headers. CORS is a browser rule for cross-origin reads, not authentication. With cookie sessions set {{SameSite}} and {{HttpOnly}} and add CSRF tokens for state-changing requests; bearer tokens in headers are not sent automatically so CSRF is less of a concern.
concepts.production: Setting {{Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *}} with credentials appeared to work in testing and was rejected by browsers in production.
concepts.interview: Say what CORS does not protect.

concepts.title: The testing trophy and what to mock
concepts.summary: Favour integration tests that exercise real code paths, with fewer pure unit tests and a thin layer of end-to-end tests. Mock only boundaries you do not own, such as third-party APIs and time, and never mock the code under test.
concepts.production: A suite with 2,000 heavily mocked unit tests passed while checkout was broken; five integration tests against a real database would have failed.
concepts.interview: Say what you would not mock, and why.

concepts.title: node:test, Jest and Vitest
concepts.summary: {{node:test}} is built in with {{describe}}, {{it}}, mocks and coverage. Jest has the biggest ecosystem; Vitest is fast and ESM-native. Pick one per repo, run tests in CI on every change and keep them fast enough that people run them locally.
concepts.production: A service moved from Jest to the built-in runner and removed a dozen dev dependencies.
concepts.interview: Be able to justify your runner choice in one sentence.

concepts.title: HTTP tests without a port: Supertest and inject
concepts.summary: Test routes by sending requests directly to the app object: Supertest for Express, {{app.inject()}} for Fastify. No ports, no flaky network, and tests can run in parallel.
concepts.production: Port collisions made CI flaky until tests used {{inject}}.
concepts.interview: Show how you assert status, body and headers for one route.

concepts.title: Real dependencies with Testcontainers
concepts.summary: Testcontainers starts disposable Postgres, Redis or Kafka containers for tests, so you run migrations and queries against the real thing instead of an in-memory fake that behaves differently.
concepts.production: A bug in a {{FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED}} job queue only reproduced against real Postgres.
concepts.interview: Explain how you isolate data between parallel test workers.

concepts.title: Contract tests and breaking-change checks
concepts.summary: Consumer-driven contract tests (for example Pact) verify that a provider still satisfies what each consumer actually uses. An OpenAPI diff in CI catches spec-level breaks, but not behavior changes such as a different default sort.
concepts.production: A changed default sort order passed the spec diff and failed only the consumer contract test.
concepts.interview: Say what each guard catches and what slips past both.

concepts.title: Flaky tests and time
concepts.summary: Flakiness comes from shared state, real clocks, real networks and ordering assumptions. Use fake timers or an injected clock, isolate data per test, avoid {{sleep}} and wait on conditions instead.
concepts.production: A test failing only around midnight compared dates built from the real clock.
concepts.interview: Describe your process for a test that fails one run in twenty.

concepts.title: Load and soak testing
concepts.summary: Use k6 or autocannon with realistic traffic shape, ramp-up and think time. Judge by p95 and p99 latency and error rate, not averages. Soak tests over hours reveal leaks and connection exhaustion that short runs miss.
concepts.production: A two-hour soak test exposed a steady memory climb that no unit test could.
concepts.interview: Name the metrics you would gate a release on.

concepts.title: End-to-end tests with Playwright
concepts.summary: Keep a small set of end-to-end tests for critical journeys such as sign-up and checkout. Prefer API-level tests for logic, use stable selectors and keep the trace viewer artifacts from CI for debugging.
concepts.production: Eight journey tests guarded every deploy while hundreds of cheaper API tests covered the rest.
concepts.interview: Say how you keep end-to-end suites from becoming slow and brittle.

concepts.title: Structured logging with pino
concepts.summary: Log JSON with a level, message and fields such as request id and user id. pino is fast because it does minimal work on the hot path. Redact secrets, never log whole request bodies and avoid {{console.log}} in production code.
concepts.production: Searching "orderId:1042" across structured logs took seconds; grepping free text took an afternoon.
concepts.interview: Explain log levels and what you never put in a log.

concepts.title: Metrics: RED and USE
concepts.summary: For services track Rate, Errors and Duration (RED). For resources track Utilisation, Saturation and Errors (USE). Use histograms for latency, and keep label cardinality low: never use user ids or raw URLs as labels.
concepts.production: A metric labelled with the raw URL created millions of time series and crashed the metrics backend.
concepts.interview: Name three metrics you would put on a service dashboard.

concepts.title: Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry
concepts.summary: A trace follows one request across services as spans, linked by the W3C {{traceparent}} header. OpenTelemetry auto-instruments HTTP, databases and queues. Load the SDK before your app code (for example with {{--import}}) and sample to control cost.
concepts.production: A trace showed 80 percent of a slow request was one downstream call nobody suspected.
concepts.interview: Explain how the trace context crosses a message queue.

concepts.title: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
concepts.summary: An SLI measures user-visible quality, an SLO sets the target (for example 99.9 percent of requests under 300 ms), and the error budget is the allowed failure. Alert on fast budget burn rather than on every cause.
concepts.production: Burn-rate alerts replaced dozens of noisy CPU alerts and woke people only for real user impact.
concepts.interview: Compute the monthly downtime allowed by 99.9 percent (about 43 minutes).

concepts.title: Health checks and graceful shutdown
concepts.summary: Liveness says the process is stuck and should restart; readiness says it can take traffic. On {{SIGTERM}} stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests, close pools and exit before the orchestrator's kill deadline. Fail readiness first so traffic drains.
concepts.production: Each deploy returned a few seconds of 502s until the app handled {{SIGTERM}} and readiness flipped before shutdown.
concepts.interview: Say why a liveness probe that checks the database is dangerous.

concepts.title: Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and bulkheads
concepts.summary: Every outbound call needs a timeout. Retry only idempotent operations, with backoff and a budget. A circuit breaker (for example opossum) stops calling a failing dependency, and bulkheads give each dependency its own pool so one cannot starve the rest.
concepts.production: A slow recommendations service exhausted the connection pool and took down checkout until it had its own timeout and bulkhead.
concepts.interview: Explain how retries amplify an outage when every layer retries.

concepts.title: Error tracking and alerting
concepts.summary: Send unhandled errors with context to a tracker such as Sentry, group by cause and attach release and request id. Alert on symptoms users feel, attach runbooks and tune out noise so alerts stay trusted.
concepts.production: Release tagging showed that one deploy introduced a new error class within minutes.
concepts.interview: Describe what makes an alert actionable.

concepts.title: Incident response and postmortems
concepts.summary: Assign an incident commander, communicate on a fixed cadence, mitigate before root-causing and keep a timeline. Afterwards write a blameless postmortem with contributing factors and action items that have owners and dates.
concepts.production: A good postmortem led to a deploy-time check that prevented the same class of outage.
concepts.interview: Prepare one incident story: detection, mitigation, root cause, prevention.

concepts.title: Measure first: the profiling toolbox
concepts.summary: Start with the symptom (p99 latency, CPU, memory) then profile. {{node --cpu-prof}} and DevTools via {{--inspect}} give flame graphs, clinic.js and 0x help find hot spots, and {{perf_hooks}} measures specific sections.
concepts.production: A flame graph showed 40 percent of CPU in a logging serializer, not the database everyone blamed.
concepts.interview: Narrate how you would find why an endpoint is slow, step by step.

concepts.title: Event loop lag and CPU hot spots
concepts.summary: Synchronous crypto, large {{JSON.parse}}, heavy regex and long loops block every request. Move CPU work to workers, stream large payloads, cap request sizes and break long loops with {{setImmediate}}.
concepts.production: Switching password hashing to async {{argon2}} and capping upload sizes removed latency spikes.
concepts.interview: Say which metric tells you the loop is blocked.

concepts.title: Memory leaks and heap snapshots
concepts.summary: Usual suspects: global caches without a bound, listeners added per request, closures holding large objects and timers never cleared. Take heap snapshots at intervals and compare retained objects to see what grows.
concepts.production: A per-request listener on a shared emitter leaked a few kilobytes each call until the pod ran out of memory every ten hours.
concepts.interview: Explain the three-snapshot technique.

concepts.title: Heap sizing and containers
concepts.summary: Set the old-space limit relative to the container limit (a common rule is about 75 percent through {{--max-old-space-size}}) so Node garbage collects before the kernel kills the process. CPU limits can throttle the event loop, so size requests carefully.
concepts.production: Pods were OOMKilled at 512 MB while Node believed it had more heap; setting the flag converted kills into slower, visible GC.
concepts.interview: Describe the difference between an OOMKill and a JavaScript heap out of memory error.

concepts.title: JSON and serialization costs
concepts.summary: {{JSON.stringify}} on large objects is CPU work on the main thread. Use schema-based serializers (Fastify), stream NDJSON for big lists, return only needed fields and avoid deep cloning on hot paths.
concepts.production: A report endpoint switched to streaming NDJSON and stopped timing out.
concepts.interview: Know why returning less data is the cheapest optimisation.

concepts.title: HTTP clients and connection pools
concepts.summary: Reuse connections with keep-alive (undici pools, or {{keepAlive}} agents). Set timeouts, limit concurrency per host and cache DNS results when lookups dominate latency.
concepts.production: Opening a new TLS connection for each call added 80 ms until a shared undici pool was used.
concepts.interview: Say what happens to latency when every outbound call opens a new connection.

concepts.title: Benchmarking correctly
concepts.summary: Warm up first, use identical hardware, report percentiles rather than averages and beware coordinated omission, where a stalled load generator hides slow responses. Treat micro-benchmarks as hypotheses to confirm under realistic load.
concepts.production: A change that looked 30 percent faster in a loop made no difference at p99 under real traffic.
concepts.interview: Explain why average latency can hide a problem.

concepts.title: Docker for Node services
concepts.summary: Use multi-stage builds, a small pinned base image, a non-root user and {{npm ci --omit=dev}}. Run Node directly or under an init (tini or {{--init}}) so signals reach it, copy {{package*.json}} first for layer caching and keep a good {{.dockerignore}}.
concepts.production: Dropping devDependencies and build tools cut an image from 1.1 GB to 180 MB and sped up every deploy.
concepts.interview: Explain why the container's main process should handle {{SIGTERM}}.

concepts.title: Kubernetes essentials for Node developers
concepts.summary: Know Deployments, Services, probes, resource requests and limits, ConfigMaps and Secrets, HPA and PodDisruptionBudgets. Run one Node process per container and scale with replicas. For I/O-bound services scale on request rate or queue depth, not only CPU.
concepts.production: A readiness probe that depended on the database removed every pod during a short database blip; separating liveness from readiness fixed it.
concepts.interview: Describe how a rolling update avoids dropping requests.

concepts.title: CI/CD and deployment strategies
concepts.summary: Build once and promote the same artifact through environments. Rolling updates are the default, blue/green swaps whole environments, canary shifts a small share of traffic first, and feature flags decouple deploy from release. Automate rollback on error-rate regression.
concepts.production: A canary at 5 percent caught a regression that would have hit all users.
concepts.interview: Choose a strategy for a risky change and justify it.

concepts.title: AWS map for a Node developer
concepts.summary: Compute: Lambda, ECS Fargate or EKS. Data: RDS or Aurora, ElastiCache, DynamoDB, S3. Messaging: SQS, SNS, EventBridge. Edge: CloudFront and WAF. Identity and secrets: IAM roles and Secrets Manager. Pair every service with its main failure mode.
concepts.production: Presigned S3 URLs moved large uploads off the API entirely.
concepts.interview: Be able to place each component of a system design on this map.

concepts.title: Serverless on Lambda
concepts.summary: Initialise clients outside the handler so warm invocations reuse them, bundle with esbuild to shrink cold starts, use RDS Proxy or a pooler for databases and set reserved concurrency to protect downstream systems. Check which Node runtime versions Lambda currently supports.
concepts.production: A traffic spike scaled Lambda faster than the database could accept connections until concurrency was capped.
concepts.interview: Explain cold starts and two ways to reduce them.

concepts.title: Infrastructure as code
concepts.summary: Describe infrastructure in Terraform or OpenTofu, CDK or Pulumi, keep state safe and shared, review changes in pull requests and detect drift. Modules and small blast radius keep changes understandable.
concepts.production: Recreating an environment from code took minutes instead of a week of manual steps.
concepts.interview: Say how you review an infrastructure change safely.

concepts.title: Cost and capacity awareness
concepts.summary: Right-size instances, autoscale on the right signal, watch data transfer and NAT costs and use caching and compression to cut egress. A senior engineer can estimate monthly cost for a design.
concepts.production: Moving chatty cross-zone traffic into one zone and adding compression cut a large share of the bill.
concepts.interview: Include a rough cost estimate in your system design answer.

concepts.title: WebSockets and scaling them
concepts.summary: WebSockets keep a stateful connection per client. To scale across instances use sticky sessions or, better, a pub/sub backplane such as Redis so any instance can reach any client. Add heartbeats, authenticate on upgrade and watch {{bufferedAmount}} for slow clients.
concepts.production: Chat messages reached only users on the same pod until a Redis adapter connected the instances.
concepts.interview: Explain what breaks when you add a second instance.

concepts.title: Server-Sent Events
concepts.summary: SSE streams events one way over plain HTTP with automatic reconnect and {{Last-Event-ID}}. It suits notifications, progress updates and streaming model output. Disable proxy buffering and send periodic comments to keep connections alive.
concepts.production: A progress bar for long exports used SSE and needed no WebSocket infrastructure.
concepts.interview: Say when SSE beats WebSockets.

concepts.title: Polling, long polling, webhooks or push
concepts.summary: Short polling is simple but wasteful, long polling reduces waste, SSE and WebSockets give push, and webhooks push server-to-server. Pick on direction, frequency and client capabilities.
concepts.production: A dashboard polled every second for rarely changing data until it moved to SSE.
concepts.interview: Give a decision rule in one sentence.

concepts.title: Edge runtimes and other JavaScript runtimes
concepts.summary: Edge platforms run V8 isolates with web-standard APIs and limited Node compatibility. Deno and Bun offer different trade-offs: Bun for speed and bundled tooling, Deno for permissions and standards. Node remains the default for ecosystem breadth and production tooling.
concepts.production: Personalised redirects ran at the edge with Hono, while the main API stayed on Node.
concepts.interview: Know what you lose at the edge: long-lived connections, native addons, some Node APIs.

concepts.title: Native addons, WebAssembly and FFI
concepts.summary: Native addons use Node-API for stable binaries, WebAssembly gives portable near-native compute, and Node 26 adds an experimental {{node:ffi}} module. Weigh build complexity and portability before leaving JavaScript.
concepts.production: An image pipeline used a Node-API library (sharp) instead of JavaScript for a tenfold speedup.
concepts.interview: Say why a native dependency complicates containers and upgrades.

concepts.title: Calling LLM APIs reliably
concepts.summary: Treat a model API like any slow, flaky dependency: timeouts, retries with backoff on 429 and 5xx, idempotency where supported, concurrency limits, cost and token tracking and a fallback plan when it is down.
concepts.production: A batch job without a concurrency cap hit provider rate limits and failed half its work.
concepts.interview: Describe how you would cap spend per user.

concepts.title: Streaming tokens to the client
concepts.summary: Stream model output through SSE or a readable stream so users see text immediately. Pass an {{AbortSignal}} so that when the client disconnects you stop the upstream request and stop paying for tokens.
concepts.production: Cancelling abandoned streams reduced model spend noticeably on a chat feature.
concepts.interview: Show how disconnect handling stops the upstream call.

concepts.title: Structured output and validation
concepts.summary: Ask for output in a JSON schema and validate it with Zod before using it. Treat the model's answer as untrusted input: retry or repair on failure and never pass it straight to a query or shell.
concepts.production: Validating tool arguments rejected a malformed id that would have reached the database.
concepts.interview: Say why validation is still needed even with a strict schema.

concepts.title: Tool calling and agent loops
concepts.summary: The model requests a function call, your code authorises and runs it, and you return the result. Cap iterations and cost, log every step as a trace and apply the user's permissions to each tool, not the model's.
concepts.production: An agent was limited to read-only tools until a human approved write actions.
concepts.interview: Explain where authorization happens in the loop.

concepts.title: RAG: retrieval-augmented generation
concepts.summary: Split documents into chunks, embed them, store vectors (pgvector or a vector database), retrieve relevant chunks per query, optionally rerank and put them in the prompt. Filter retrieval by the user's access rights and measure retrieval quality, not only answer quality.
concepts.production: A support bot answered from stale pages until documents were re-indexed on change.
concepts.interview: Describe how you would keep permissions correct in retrieval.

concepts.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers
concepts.summary: MCP is an open protocol for exposing tools and data to AI clients. You can implement a server in TypeScript with the official SDK. Validate tool inputs, authenticate callers and expose the least capability necessary.
concepts.production: An internal MCP server let an assistant look up order status through a read-only, audited endpoint.
concepts.interview: Treat tool inputs like any external request: validate and authorise.

concepts.title: Prompt injection and exfiltration
concepts.summary: Text from documents, web pages or emails can contain instructions aimed at the model. Limit tool power, separate trusted instructions from untrusted content, filter outputs, require approval for sensitive actions and never put secrets in prompts.
concepts.production: A summarised web page told the assistant to email a document; a human-approval gate for sending mail stopped it.
concepts.interview: Name two controls that reduce the blast radius.

concepts.title: A repeatable design framework
concepts.summary: Clarify requirements, estimate load, define the API, sketch the data model, draw the high-level design, deep-dive the riskiest parts, then discuss failures, scaling and trade-offs. Say your assumptions aloud.
concepts.production: Candidates who skipped estimates designed a distributed system for 20 requests a second.
concepts.interview: Narrate each step and ask clarifying questions before drawing.

concepts.title: Back-of-envelope estimation
concepts.summary: One million requests a day is about 12 per second on average; plan for a peak of two to five times. Estimate storage as items times size times retention times replication, and measure instance capacity with a load test instead of guessing.
concepts.production: An estimate showed a feature needed one database, not a cluster, which saved months.
concepts.interview: Use the capacity calculator in the labs section.

concepts.title: Caching, CDN and read scaling
concepts.summary: Layer caches: browser, CDN, application memory, Redis, database. Decide what is cacheable, how it invalidates and what stale data is acceptable. Add read replicas when reads dominate and watch replica lag.
concepts.production: A public catalogue behind a CDN served the vast majority of traffic without touching the API.
concepts.interview: Say what you cache and how it becomes invalid.

concepts.title: Designing a rate limiter or gateway
concepts.summary: Pick an algorithm (token bucket or sliding window), store counters in Redis with atomic operations, decide the key (user, API key, IP, route) and the response ({{429}} with {{Retry-After}}). Consider failing open or closed when the store is down.
concepts.production: Per-tenant limits stopped one noisy customer from degrading others.
concepts.interview: State your fail-open versus fail-closed choice and why.

concepts.title: File uploads and media pipelines
concepts.summary: Issue presigned URLs so clients upload directly to object storage, then trigger asynchronous processing (virus scan, resize, transcode) through events, and serve results through a CDN. Use resumable uploads for large files.
concepts.production: Direct-to-S3 uploads removed multi-gigabyte request bodies from the API tier.
concepts.interview: Explain why the API should not proxy large uploads.

concepts.title: Payments and ledger correctness
concepts.summary: Model payment state as an explicit state machine, use idempotency keys with the provider, record money movements in a double-entry ledger, verify webhooks and reconcile against provider reports regularly.
concepts.production: A nightly reconciliation job found captured payments that never reached the ledger after a webhook outage.
concepts.interview: Say how you detect and repair a mismatch.

concepts.title: Multi-tenancy
concepts.summary: Options: shared tables with a {{tenant_id}} column (enforced by row-level security), schema per tenant or database per tenant. The more isolation, the higher the cost and operational load. Add per-tenant rate limits and quotas to contain noisy neighbours.
concepts.production: Row-level security prevented a missing {{WHERE tenant_id}} from leaking data across customers.
concepts.interview: Choose an isolation level for a given customer profile and defend it.

concepts.title: Code review that scales
concepts.summary: Review for correctness, clarity, tests and risk, not style (automate style). Keep changes small, comment on design early and say what is blocking versus optional. Good review is a teaching tool.
concepts.production: Splitting a 2,000-line change into stacked small pull requests turned slow reviews into same-day ones.
concepts.interview: Describe how you review a large change.

concepts.title: Design docs and architecture decision records
concepts.summary: A short design doc states the problem, options considered, trade-offs and the decision. ADRs record decisions and their context so future engineers understand why. Writing clarifies thinking and invites early feedback.
concepts.production: An ADR explaining why a queue was chosen saved a re-debate a year later.
concepts.interview: Bring an example of a decision you documented.

concepts.title: Estimating and slicing work
concepts.summary: Break work into thin vertical slices that deliver value, surface unknowns early with spikes, give ranges instead of single numbers and re-estimate as you learn.
concepts.production: Slicing a migration by route group delivered value weekly instead of one risky big bang.
concepts.interview: Explain how you communicate uncertainty to a manager.

concepts.title: Owning production: on-call and runbooks
concepts.summary: Own what you ship: dashboards, alerts, runbooks and an on-call rotation that is sustainable. Fix the causes of pages, not just the symptoms, and invest in automation that removes toil.
concepts.production: Documenting the top five alerts as runbooks cut average resolution time for new on-call engineers.
concepts.interview: Share how you reduced alert noise.

concepts.title: Managing technical debt and upgrades
concepts.summary: Track debt visibly, pay it down continuously and tie it to business risk. Automate dependency updates with Renovate or Dependabot, keep a regular runtime upgrade cadence and remove unused code.
concepts.production: Staying one LTS behind made the move to the next one a routine change instead of a project.
concepts.interview: Explain how you persuade stakeholders to fund an upgrade.

concepts.title: Using AI coding tools responsibly
concepts.summary: Treat generated code as a draft from a junior colleague: read it, test it, understand it and never paste secrets or private data. Strong tests and types are the guardrails that make assisted development safe.
concepts.production: An assistant produced plausible but vulnerable SQL; a review and a parameterised-query rule caught it.
concepts.interview: Say how you verify generated code before merging.

concepts.title: Mentoring and communicating trade-offs
concepts.summary: Explain decisions in terms of risk, cost and user impact, tailor depth to the audience, and grow others by delegating real ownership with support. Seniority is measured by the engineers you make better.
concepts.production: A principal engineer paired a junior on an incident so they learned the diagnostic path, not just the fix.
concepts.interview: Prepare a story about raising someone else's level.

questions.q: How do you choose a Node.js version for production?
questions.a: Run Active or Maintenance LTS only. Today that means Node 24, with Node 26 becoming LTS on 28 October 2026 and Node 22 supported until April 2027. Node 20 is end of life. Test the Current line in CI, upgrade within a few months of LTS and block on deprecation warnings.

questions.q: What recent Node.js features let you remove dependencies?
questions.a: Global {{fetch}}, {{node:test}}, {{--watch}}, {{--env-file}}, {{AbortSignal.timeout}}, {{structuredClone}}, {{util.parseArgs}} and native TypeScript type stripping. Fewer dependencies means a smaller attack surface and faster installs, but only drop a package when the built-in meets your needs.

questions.q: How do ESM and CommonJS interoperate, and what breaks?
questions.a: ESM can import CommonJS (default export is {{module.exports}}). CommonJS can {{require()}} ESM in recent LTS lines if it has no top-level await. Breakages: missing file extensions, {{__dirname}} absent in ESM, and dual-package hazards where two copies of a module hold separate state.

questions.q: What does native TypeScript execution in Node not give you?
questions.a: It only erases types: no type checking, no enums, namespaces or parameter properties, no path aliases and no downlevel transforms. Keep {{tsc --noEmit}} in CI, use {{erasableSyntaxOnly}}, and still bundle or build when you need source maps or startup optimisation.

questions.q: Why validate input with Zod when you already use TypeScript?
questions.a: Types exist only at compile time. Data from HTTP, queues and environment variables is untyped at runtime. A schema validates at the boundary and infers the TypeScript type, so runtime checks and static types cannot drift.

questions.q: What do strict and noUncheckedIndexedAccess add?
questions.a: {{strict}} enables null checks and implicit any errors. {{noUncheckedIndexedAccess}} makes {{arr[i]}} possibly undefined, forcing you to handle empty or missing entries instead of crashing at runtime.

questions.q: Explain discriminated unions and why they help.
questions.a: A union of object types sharing a literal tag field. Switching on the tag narrows the type, and a {{never}} assignment in the default branch fails compilation when a new variant is unhandled. It makes impossible states unrepresentable.

questions.q: What order do nextTick, promises, setTimeout and setImmediate run in?
questions.a: Synchronous code first. Then {{process.nextTick}} callbacks, then promise microtasks. From the main module, {{setTimeout(0)}} versus {{setImmediate}} is not guaranteed, but inside an I/O callback {{setImmediate}} runs first. Starving microtasks blocks I/O.

questions.q: What happens with an unhandled promise rejection?
questions.a: Since Node 15 the default is to throw, which crashes the process. Always {{await}} or attach {{.catch}}, and register a last-resort handler that logs and exits so the orchestrator restarts a clean process.

questions.q: How do you limit concurrency across thousands of async tasks?
questions.a: Use a pool such as p-limit, or process in bounded batches. Unbounded {{Promise.all}} exhausts sockets and rate limits. For streams rely on backpressure instead of buffering.

questions.q: How do you cancel work and enforce timeouts?
questions.a: Create an {{AbortSignal}} with {{AbortSignal.timeout(ms)}}, combine signals with {{AbortSignal.any}}, and pass it to {{fetch}}, {{timers/promises}} and drivers that accept it. Propagate it downstream so cancelling the request stops the work behind it.

questions.q: When do you use worker threads, child processes or cluster?
questions.a: Worker threads for CPU-bound JavaScript within one process, child processes for external programs or isolation, and cluster or more containers to use more cores for I/O-bound services. In Kubernetes, prefer more single-process containers.

questions.q: What is AsyncLocalStorage and what can go wrong?
questions.a: It propagates context such as a request id across async boundaries. Pitfalls: context lost when work runs outside the store (for example callbacks registered at startup) and misuse as hidden global state. It underpins log correlation and tracing.

questions.q: Explain idempotency keys.
questions.a: The client sends a unique key with a write. The server records the key and request fingerprint, executes once and replays the stored response for repeats. Enforce with a unique constraint and handle the in-progress state so concurrent duplicates do not both run.

questions.q: PUT versus PATCH versus POST?
questions.a: PUT replaces a resource and is idempotent. PATCH applies a partial change and may or may not be idempotent. POST creates or triggers an action and is not idempotent by default.

questions.q: How do ETags and caching headers work together?
questions.a: {{Cache-Control}} sets how long a response is fresh. When stale, the client sends {{If-None-Match}} with the ETag and the server returns 304 if unchanged, saving bandwidth. {{Vary}} lists request headers that change the response.

questions.q: Why cursor pagination over offset?
questions.a: Offset skips rows, which gets slower with depth and shifts when data changes, causing duplicates or gaps. A cursor on a stable ordering such as {{(created_at, id)}} is fast and consistent.

questions.q: How do you design a webhook receiver?
questions.a: Capture the raw body, verify an HMAC with a timing-safe compare, check the timestamp window, return 2xx quickly and process asynchronously. Make handlers idempotent and tolerant of reordering because delivery is at-least-once.

questions.q: REST, GraphQL, gRPC or tRPC: how do you choose?
questions.a: REST for public, cacheable resources; GraphQL when clients need flexible shapes and you can manage query cost and N+1; gRPC for internal low-latency typed calls; tRPC when one team owns a TypeScript client and server. Decide by consumers, caching and language mix.

questions.q: Why do you see sporadic 502s from a load balancer with clean app logs?
questions.a: Node's {{keepAliveTimeout}} (5 seconds by default) can be shorter than the balancer's idle timeout. The balancer reuses a socket Node already closed. Raise {{keepAliveTimeout}} above the balancer timeout and {{headersTimeout}} slightly above that.

questions.q: Express, Fastify or NestJS?
questions.a: Express: minimal and familiar. Fastify: schema-first, fast, built-in validation and logging. NestJS: modules and DI for large teams. Pick by team conventions and requirements; framework overhead rarely dominates real handlers.

questions.q: What is hexagonal architecture and what does it cost?
questions.a: The domain depends on ports (interfaces) and adapters implement them for HTTP, databases and queues. You can test the domain in isolation and swap infrastructure. Cost: more files and indirection, which is not worthwhile for tiny services.

questions.q: Why start with a modular monolith?
questions.a: It keeps one deployable and one database while enforcing module boundaries. You avoid network failures, distributed transactions and heavy observability needs until scale or team structure justify splitting.

questions.q: How do you manage configuration safely?
questions.a: Read environment variables, validate them with a schema at startup, fail fast on errors and keep secrets in a secret manager. The same build artifact runs in every environment.

questions.q: Explain isolation levels and a lost update.
questions.a: READ COMMITTED (Postgres default) can allow non-repeatable reads. Two transactions reading then writing the same row can overwrite each other (lost update). Fix with {{SELECT ... FOR UPDATE}}, atomic updates, optimistic version checks or stricter isolation with retries.

questions.q: How do you decide a connection pool size?
questions.a: Multiply pool size by pod count and keep the total under {{max_connections}} with headroom for admin and migrations. Use PgBouncer for many clients, and size from measured concurrency rather than guessing.

questions.q: Prisma, Drizzle, Kysely or raw SQL?
questions.a: Prisma gives productivity and migrations; Drizzle and Kysely keep SQL explicit with typed results. All can produce N+1 queries if misused. Choose on type safety, escape hatches and migration workflow, and always be able to read the generated SQL.

questions.q: How do you rename a column with zero downtime?
questions.a: Expand and contract: add the new column, write to both, backfill in batches, switch reads, stop writing the old one, then drop it in a later release. Create indexes concurrently and keep each step reversible.

questions.q: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: Many requests recompute the same expired value at once. Prevent with TTL jitter, single-flight or locks, serving stale while refreshing, and pre-warming hot keys.

questions.q: When embed and when reference in MongoDB?
questions.a: Embed data read together and bounded in size. Reference data that is shared, large or unbounded. Watch document size limits and update patterns.

questions.q: How do you handle duplicate message delivery?
questions.a: Assume at-least-once delivery. Make consumers idempotent by storing processed message ids or using upserts and unique constraints, so processing twice has the same effect as once.

questions.q: What is the outbox pattern?
questions.a: Write the data change and an event row in one local transaction. A separate relay publishes outbox rows to the broker and marks them sent. This avoids losing events when the database commits but a direct publish fails.

questions.q: Orchestrated versus choreographed sagas?
questions.a: Orchestration uses a coordinator that commands each step and handles compensation, which is easier to follow and monitor. Choreography lets services react to events, which reduces coupling but makes the overall flow harder to see.

questions.q: How does ordering work in Kafka?
questions.a: Order is guaranteed within a partition only. Use a key such as the entity id so related events land in one partition. Consumer parallelism is limited by partition count.

questions.q: What is a dead-letter queue for?
questions.a: It holds messages that failed after the allowed retries, so they stop blocking the queue. Alert on its depth, inspect the cause and replay once fixed.

questions.q: What is broken object level authorization?
questions.a: A user accesses another user's object by changing an identifier because the server checked authentication but not ownership. Check authorization for the specific object on every request.

questions.q: What are the main JWT pitfalls?
questions.a: Not verifying the algorithm, long lifetimes without revocation, storing tokens in {{localStorage}} (XSS risk) and putting sensitive data in the payload. Use short-lived access tokens with rotating refresh tokens.

questions.q: How do you defend against supply-chain attacks?
questions.a: Commit the lockfile and use {{npm ci}}, review new dependencies, limit install scripts, verify provenance, delay adopting fresh releases, use phishing-resistant 2FA for publishing and give CI tokens minimal scope.

questions.q: How is SSRF prevented?
questions.a: Allow-list destination hosts, block private and metadata IP ranges after DNS resolution, disable redirects or revalidate them, and run fetchers with minimal network access.

questions.q: CORS versus CSRF?
questions.a: CORS is a browser mechanism that controls cross-origin reads; it is not authentication. CSRF abuses automatically attached cookies, so use {{SameSite}} cookies and CSRF tokens. Bearer tokens in headers are not auto-sent.

questions.q: Why are regexes a security concern in Node?
questions.a: Catastrophic backtracking on hostile input can pin the single thread and deny service to everyone. Use linear-time engines or safe patterns, limit input size and test with adversarial strings.

questions.q: What should you mock in tests?
questions.a: Boundaries you do not own, such as third-party APIs and time. Do not mock the code under test or things cheap to run for real, like a database in a container.

questions.q: How do you handle a flaky test?
questions.a: Find the shared state, time, network or ordering dependence. Inject a clock, isolate data per test, wait on conditions instead of sleeping, and quarantine with a ticket rather than ignoring.

questions.q: What do contract tests catch that OpenAPI diffs miss?
questions.a: Behavioral changes the spec does not describe, such as a default sort order or field semantics. Consumer-driven contracts verify what each consumer actually relies on.

questions.q: Why use Testcontainers?
questions.a: It runs real Postgres, Redis or Kafka in disposable containers so tests exercise real behaviour (locks, constraints, ordering) rather than a fake that behaves differently.

questions.q: What are RED and USE?
questions.a: RED for services: Rate, Errors, Duration. USE for resources: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors. Together they cover user-facing health and underlying capacity.

questions.q: How do SLOs and error budgets guide work?
questions.a: The SLO sets an acceptable level of unreliability. When the budget is healthy you ship faster; when it burns quickly you prioritise reliability. Alerts fire on burn rate, tying paging to user impact.

questions.q: How should a Node service shut down gracefully?
questions.a: On SIGTERM fail readiness, stop accepting connections, wait for in-flight requests, close databases, queues and caches, then exit before the orchestrator's kill deadline.

questions.q: How do retries make outages worse and how do you control them?
questions.a: If every layer retries, load multiplies exactly when a dependency struggles. Retry only idempotent calls, use backoff with jitter, cap attempts, apply retry budgets and add circuit breakers.

questions.q: How does trace context cross a message queue?
questions.a: Inject the W3C {{traceparent}} into message headers when publishing and extract it in the consumer to start a linked span. OpenTelemetry instrumentation can do this automatically for many brokers.

questions.q: An endpoint's p99 is high. How do you investigate?
questions.a: Confirm with percentile metrics, check event loop delay, profile with {{--cpu-prof}} or a flame graph, inspect database queries and downstream calls with traces, form a hypothesis, change one thing and measure again.

questions.q: How do you find a memory leak?
questions.a: Watch the memory slope, take heap snapshots at intervals and compare retained objects to see what grows, then follow retainer paths to the owner (global map, listener or closure). Fix and verify with a soak test.

questions.q: Why can average latency mislead?
questions.a: Averages hide the slow tail that real users hit, and load generators can hide stalls (coordinated omission). Report p95 and p99, and measure under realistic concurrency.

questions.q: What makes a good Dockerfile for Node?
questions.a: Multi-stage build, pinned small base image, non-root user, {{npm ci --omit=dev}}, dependency files copied first for caching, a {{.dockerignore}} and proper signal handling.

questions.q: Liveness versus readiness probes?
questions.a: Liveness restarts a stuck process; readiness removes a pod from traffic when it cannot serve. Do not let liveness depend on external services, or an outage will restart every pod.

questions.q: Blue/green versus canary?
questions.a: Blue/green switches all traffic between two environments for quick rollback. Canary sends a small share to the new version first and compares metrics, which limits blast radius. Feature flags decouple release from deploy.

questions.q: What are Lambda cold starts and how do you reduce them?
questions.a: A cold start is the init time when a new execution environment starts. Reduce it by bundling with esbuild, shrinking dependencies, initialising clients outside the handler, and using provisioned concurrency for latency-critical paths.

questions.q: How do you scale WebSockets across instances?
questions.a: Use a pub/sub backplane such as Redis so any instance can deliver to any connected client, or sticky sessions with care. Add heartbeats, authenticate on upgrade and handle backpressure from slow clients.

questions.q: SSE or WebSockets?
questions.a: SSE for one-way server-to-client streams over HTTP with automatic reconnect, such as notifications or token streaming. WebSockets for two-way, low-latency interaction.

questions.q: How do you stream LLM output and handle disconnects?
questions.a: Forward tokens through SSE or a readable stream. Wire the client's disconnect to an {{AbortController}} so you cancel the upstream request and stop paying for unused tokens.

questions.q: How do you defend against prompt injection?
questions.a: Assume untrusted content can carry instructions. Limit tool permissions, separate trusted instructions from data, validate outputs, require human approval for sensitive actions and never put secrets in prompts.

questions.q: Outline a RAG pipeline.
questions.a: Chunk documents, embed chunks, store vectors, retrieve top matches per query (filtered by the user's permissions), optionally rerank, then prompt the model with the context. Evaluate retrieval quality and keep the index fresh.

questions.q: Design a rate limiter.
questions.a: Choose token bucket or sliding window, store counters in Redis with atomic operations, key by user or API key, return {{429}} with {{Retry-After}} and decide fail-open or fail-closed when Redis is unreachable. Add per-tenant limits.

questions.q: Design a file upload service.
questions.a: Issue presigned URLs for direct upload to object storage, emit an event on completion, process asynchronously (scan, resize) and serve through a CDN. Support resumable uploads for large files.

questions.q: How do you choose a multi-tenancy model?
questions.a: Shared tables with tenant_id and row-level security are cheapest; schema per tenant balances isolation; database per tenant gives the strongest isolation at the highest operational cost. Choose by compliance, scale and noisy-neighbour risk.

questions.q: How do you handle a disagreement with another senior engineer?
questions.a: Align on goals and constraints, make options and trade-offs explicit in writing, test assumptions with a small spike or data, and escalate for a decision only when needed. Commit to the outcome once decided.

questions.q: How do you decide when to pay down technical debt?
questions.a: Tie it to risk and cost: incidents, slow delivery or security exposure. Make it visible, schedule it continuously and show outcomes in business terms.

questions.q: How do you raise the engineers around you?
