questions.a: Delegate real ownership with support, review for teaching, document decisions, pair on hard problems and give specific feedback. Measure success by what others can now do without you.

drills.title: p99 latency spikes every few minutes
drills.context: An orders API shows p99 latency jumping from 120 ms to 2 s every few minutes. Average CPU is 35 percent, database dashboards look healthy and adding pods did not help.
symptoms: Spikes are periodic and affect unrelated endpoints on the same pod
CPU averages look fine but individual cores spike
Database query times are normal

options.why: Database metrics are healthy and unrelated endpoints are affected.

options.text: Synchronous work is blocking the event loop
options.why: One slow synchronous task (large JSON parse, regex or hashing) delays every request on that process.
More pods did not change the spikes, which points to per-process blocking.
Jitter would not be periodic or tied to a single process.

path: Graph event loop delay (monitorEventLoopDelay) and correlate with spikes
Capture a CPU profile with --cpu-prof or clinic flame during a spike
Find the synchronous hot spot, such as a nightly report parsing a huge payload
drills.fix: Stream or paginate the large payload, move CPU-heavy work to a worker pool, cap request sizes and make any regex linear-time.
drills.prevent: Alert on event loop p99 delay, set body size limits and add a load test with realistic payloads.
drills.interview: Say the diagnostic order: measure loop lag first, profile second, change code third.

drills.title: Customers charged twice
drills.context: After a mobile release, support reports duplicate orders and double card charges. Logs show two identical POST requests a few seconds apart.
symptoms: Duplicates cluster on slow mobile networks
Each request succeeded individually
No errors in the logs

options.why: The two requests are genuinely separate; the root cause is why they were sent.

options.text: The client retried after a timeout and the endpoint is not idempotent
options.why: A timed-out request is retried by the client or SDK, and the server processed both.
The balancer forwarded two real requests sent by the client.
Caches do not create new orders.

path: Compare request ids and client timestamps on the duplicate pair
Confirm the first request completed server-side after the client timed out
Check whether the endpoint accepts an idempotency key
drills.fix: Require an Idempotency-Key header, store key plus request fingerprint plus result with a unique constraint and replay the saved response on duplicates.
drills.prevent: Add idempotency to every endpoint that creates money-moving side effects and test retries with a chaos or network-fault tool.
drills.interview: Describe the three states of a key: new, in progress, completed.

drills.title: Pods restart every ten hours
drills.context: A service is OOMKilled roughly every ten hours. Memory climbs steadily between restarts and drops after each deploy.
symptoms: Resident memory grows linearly with traffic
Restarts correlate with a fixed memory limit
No spike, just a slope

options.why: A steady slope that resets on restart is the classic leak signature.

options.text: A CPU limit that is too low
options.why: CPU throttling slows work but does not grow memory.
Slow queries do not produce a smooth memory ramp.
Pod count does not change per-process memory growth.

path: Take heap snapshots at start, after an hour and after a few hours
Compare retained objects and look at growth by constructor
Follow retainers to the owner, often a global Map, listeners or closures
drills.fix: Bound or evict the cache, remove per-request listeners, clear timers and avoid holding request objects in long-lived structures.
drills.prevent: Run soak tests, alert on memory slope and set the heap limit below the container limit so GC acts first.
drills.interview: Explain the three-snapshot technique and what a retainer path tells you.

drills.title: Database refuses connections after autoscaling
drills.context: Traffic doubled and the platform scaled the API from 8 to 40 pods. Within minutes, requests fail with "too many clients already".
symptoms: Failures begin right after scale-out
Database CPU is low
Each pod uses a pool of 20 connections

options.text: A pool per pod multiplied past max_connections
options.why: 40 pods times a pool of 20 is 800 connections, beyond the database limit.

options.text: The database ran out of CPU
options.why: CPU is low; this is connection exhaustion.
Locks cause waits, not a connection count error.
DNS errors look different and would not reference clients.

path: Multiply pods by pool size and compare with max_connections
Check idle versus active connections in pg_stat_activity
Look for long-held transactions or leaked clients
drills.fix: Add PgBouncer in transaction mode, reduce pool sizes and cap the autoscaler maximum so the connection budget always holds.
drills.prevent: Treat connections as a budget in capacity reviews and alert when usage passes 70 percent.
drills.interview: Do the multiplication aloud before answering anything else.

drills.title: The nightly cache expiry melts the database
drills.context: Every night around 03:00 the database CPU jumps to 100 percent for about 30 seconds and the API times out.
symptoms: Happens at the same time daily
Cache hit ratio drops to zero then recovers
Queries are identical and numerous

options.why: GC pauses are shorter and not tied to a clock time.

options.text: A cache stampede after keys expire together
options.why: Keys with the same TTL expire at once and every request recomputes the same data.
A partition would not recover by itself in 30 seconds with identical queries.
Disk problems are not scheduled to a time of day.

path: Check cache hit ratio and key expiry times around the incident
Look for identical queries issued concurrently
Confirm TTLs were set from one batch fill
drills.fix: Add random jitter to TTLs, coalesce concurrent loads with single-flight or a lock and serve stale data while refreshing in the background.
drills.prevent: Pre-warm hot keys, load test cache cold-start and alert on sudden hit ratio drops.
drills.interview: Name three defences: jitter, single-flight, stale-while-revalidate.

drills.title: A bad message blocks the queue
drills.context: Queue depth keeps growing while one consumer logs the same error repeatedly. Other messages wait behind it.
symptoms: Same message id appears in logs over and over
Consumer throughput drops to nearly zero
No alerts fired

options.text: A poison message is retried forever
options.why: A permanently failing message is redelivered and blocks progress without a retry limit or DLQ.
The broker is delivering the same message, so it is up.
More consumers would hit the same poison message in turn.
Skew does not cause identical repeated failures.

path: Identify the repeating message id and its payload
Classify the error as transient or permanent
Check retry settings and whether a DLQ exists
drills.fix: Cap attempts with exponential backoff and jitter, move failures to a dead-letter queue and replay after fixing the cause.
drills.prevent: Alert on DLQ depth and consumer lag, validate messages at consume time and keep handlers idempotent.
drills.interview: Describe a retry policy per error class.

drills.title: Webhooks leave subscriptions in the wrong state
drills.context: A billing provider sends subscription events. Occasionally a customer shows as cancelled although they are active.
symptoms: Happens when two events arrive close together
Both events were processed successfully
The final state matches the older event

options.text: Events arrived out of order and the older one won
options.why: Providers retry and deliver out of order; blindly applying each event overwrites newer state.
Ordering is not guaranteed by design.
A deadlock would produce errors, not silent wrong state.
Both events were received and processed.

path: Compare event timestamps or sequence numbers with processing order
Check whether handlers upsert or overwrite blindly
Reproduce by replaying two events in reverse
drills.fix: Store a version or event time, ignore events older than the stored state, or fetch the latest object from the provider API when handling an event. Keep handlers idempotent.
drills.prevent: Test out-of-order and duplicate deliveries and reconcile state nightly against the provider.
drills.interview: Say that webhooks give at-least-once, unordered delivery.

drills.title: Sporadic 502s with a clean application log
drills.context: Behind an AWS load balancer, a small percentage of requests return 502. The Node application logs no errors for them.
symptoms: Failure rate is low and random
Application metrics show nothing
Happens more at lower traffic

options.why: A crash would appear in logs and restarts.

options.text: Node closes idle connections before the load balancer does
options.why: Node default keepAliveTimeout is 5 seconds; the balancer idle timeout is longer, so it reuses sockets Node just closed.
That would show OOM events.
DNS issues give connection errors, not 502 from the balancer.

path: Compare the balancer idle timeout with server.keepAliveTimeout
Check balancer logs for target connection reset
Note it is more likely at low traffic when sockets sit idle
drills.fix: Set server.keepAliveTimeout above the balancer idle timeout and headersTimeout slightly above that.
drills.prevent: Document timeouts for every hop and review them whenever infrastructure changes.
drills.interview: Use this as your example of a bug only visible between layers.

incidents.title: left-pad, March 2016
incidents.body: A maintainer unpublished a tiny package and builds around the world broke. npm later restricted unpublishing. Lesson: lockfiles, a registry mirror and awareness of how deep a dependency tree goes.

incidents.title: event-stream, 2018
incidents.body: Maintenance of a popular package was handed to a stranger who added a malicious dependency that targeted a cryptocurrency wallet. Lesson: trust is transitive; audit new maintainers and updates.

incidents.title: Cloudflare outage, July 2019
incidents.body: A regular expression with catastrophic backtracking in a WAF rule pinned CPUs and caused a global outage. Lesson: regexes can be denial of service, and risky changes need staged rollout.

incidents.title: npm phishing and worm, September 2025
incidents.body: A maintainer was phished and 18 widely used packages, including chalk and debug, shipped malicious versions for hours. A self-replicating worm then spread through hundreds of packages. Lesson: phishing-resistant 2FA, pinned lockfiles and release-age delays.

architecture.name: Client
architecture.role: Browser or mobile app. Sends requests with timeouts and retries.
architecture.risk: Retry storms from many clients after an outage.
architecture.question: What should the client do when it gets a 429 or 503?

architecture.name: CDN and WAF
architecture.role: Caches public content, terminates TLS at the edge and blocks abusive traffic.
architecture.risk: Stale content after a deploy; overly strict WAF rules blocking real users.
architecture.question: What do you cache at the edge and how do you purge it?

architecture.name: Load balancer
architecture.role: Distributes requests, runs health checks and enforces idle timeouts.
architecture.risk: Idle timeout shorter than Node keepAliveTimeout causes 502s.
architecture.question: How does the balancer know a pod is ready, and what happens during a deploy?

architecture.name: API pods (Node)
architecture.role: Stateless Node processes: validate input, authorise, call data stores, publish events.
architecture.risk: Event loop blocking, memory leaks, missing timeouts on downstream calls.
architecture.question: How do you keep these pods stateless and safe to kill at any time?

architecture.name: Cache (Redis)
architecture.role: Fast reads, counters, rate limits and locks.
architecture.risk: Stampede on expiry, evictions under memory pressure, treated as a source of truth.
architecture.question: What happens to the system when the cache is empty or down?

architecture.name: Database (Postgres)
architecture.role: Source of truth with transactions. Primary for writes, replicas for reads.
architecture.risk: Connection exhaustion, long transactions, replica lag, slow queries.
architecture.question: How do you size pools and migrate without downtime?

architecture.name: Queue or broker
architecture.role: Decouples slow or unreliable work from requests; delivers at least once.
architecture.risk: Poison messages, unbounded backlog, duplicate delivery.
architecture.question: How do consumers stay idempotent and how do you replay?

architecture.name: Workers (Node)
architecture.role: Consume jobs, call third parties, retry with backoff and report results.
architecture.risk: Double execution on multiple pods, no timeouts, silent failures.
architecture.question: How do you scale workers and protect downstream systems?

architecture.name: Observability
architecture.role: Structured logs, metrics, traces and alerts across every component.
architecture.risk: High-cardinality labels, missing correlation ids, noisy alerts.
architecture.question: How would you find the cause of one slow request across services?

glance.title: Event loop order
glance.text: After each macrotask: nextTick, then promise microtasks. Timers, I/O poll, then check (setImmediate).

glance.title: Unhandled rejections
glance.text: Crash the process by default since Node 15. Always await or catch.

glance.title: Backpressure
glance.text: Pause the producer when the consumer is slow. Use stream pipeline, not bare pipe.

glance.title: Idempotency
glance.text: Retries are certain. Key plus unique constraint plus replay makes writes safe.

glance.title: keepAliveTimeout
glance.text: Keep Node above the load balancer idle timeout to avoid sporadic 502s.

glance.title: Pool arithmetic
glance.text: Pods times pool size must fit under the database max_connections.

glance.title: JWT pitfalls
glance.text: Short-lived access tokens, rotating refresh tokens, no secrets in payload, verify the algorithm.

glance.title: Outbox and sagas
glance.text: No dual writes: commit the event with the data; compensate instead of distributed transactions.

glance.title: Graceful shutdown
glance.text: On SIGTERM fail readiness, stop accepting, drain in-flight, close pools, exit before SIGKILL.

glance.title: N+1 and p99
glance.text: Batch or join relations. Judge latency by percentiles, not averages.

glance.title: Object level authorization
glance.text: Check that the caller owns the object on every request, not just that they are logged in.

lists.title: Live coding tips
items: Restate the problem and confirm inputs, outputs and limits
Start with the simplest correct version, then improve
Talk through your reasoning continuously
Write a quick test or walk an example, including empty input
Handle errors and cancellation instead of ignoring them
If stuck, say what you know and propose a smaller step

lists.title: Take-home tips
items: Time-box it and state what you left out
Include a README with setup, decisions and trade-offs
Add tests for the core behaviour and one failure path
Validate input and return consistent errors
Keep dependencies few and commit history readable
Mention what you would do with more time

lists.title: Questions to ask them
items: How often do you deploy and how do you roll back?
What does on-call look like and how often are people paged?
How are technical decisions made and documented?
What does the first quarter look like for this role?
How do you handle upgrades such as Node LTS moves?
What is the biggest technical risk right now?

lists.title: Red flags in answers
items: Saying Node is single-threaded without the thread pool nuance
Proposing microservices for a small team without costs
No timeouts, retries or failure handling in a design
Memorised buzzwords with no example from your work
Blaming people instead of describing process fixes
Ignoring monitoring and rollback in a design

stories.title: Cut p99 latency from 2.4 s to 380 ms
parts: Situation: our reports API timed out for large customers.
Task: I owned the endpoint and the latency target.
Action: event loop delay graphs pointed to synchronous serialisation. I moved export to streamed NDJSON, offloaded aggregation to a worker pool and added a loop lag alert.
Result: p99 fell from 2.4 s to 380 ms and timeouts disappeared.
Learning: measure first; I now add loop lag to every new service dashboard.

stories.title: Stopped duplicate charges
parts: Situation: retries on mobile caused double charges for about one in a thousand orders.
Task: eliminate duplicates without hurting conversion.
Action: introduced idempotency keys with a unique constraint, an outbox for events and a nightly reconciliation job.
Result: zero duplicate charges in the following quarter; support tickets on the topic dropped sharply.
Learning: design every write for retry from the start.

stories.title: Led a safe framework migration
parts: Situation: a core service on an old framework blocked upgrades and slowed delivery.
Task: migrate without downtime or a freeze.
Action: wrapped the old app inside the new framework, moved route groups one at a time behind flags, kept contract tests as the safety net and reported progress weekly.
Result: finished in ten weeks with no customer-visible incidents and faster builds.
Learning: incremental migration with strong tests beats a rewrite.
